Learn how to use Excel like a champ. Pivot tables, VLOOKUPS, even a Macro or two.

If you can be the office Excel whiz, you have a job for life. We have all this data available in business, but often very few or no way to turn it into information.

Don't know how relevant Excel will be in 20 years. Data analysis is going to become more and more automated with increasingly simplified tools, with even data entry clerks being replaced by OCR and other software.

Off the cuff data analysis not built by a report writer will always be in need.

No matter the data entry point, the info needed rarely meets the report filters, and excel based tools will not be being replaced by on the fly database queries into a format better than Excel. I just don;t see allowing every pencil pusher direct access to your database to run whatever queries thy want. It's a recipe for disaster.

I was thinking more along the lines of a program which accesses the database and sorts the data as needed which can also provide whatever access control the business deems appropriate. A PHP application simple enough for a kid to use could probably put most data analysts out of a job, especially when a company has very consistent needs.

I can see your point.

It's the "very consistent" part that I am advocating the Excel on - rarely have business needs been consistent, in my experience. Managers, executives, supervisors, and end users all have differing needs. They have different data roll-up needs, they have different levels of data, and inevitably, need to consolidate/sort/slice for different operating requirements. I have also seen these needs change monthly, if not daily - as they tackle a new issue, or try to implement a new program, or get new direction from above, the data analysis needs change.

For example, let's say your main report lists sales, grouped by category. You run ANOTHER report that provides Returns by Category. Then you have another report that lists a count of Return reasons, also by category. The manager goes to a store, sees some bad merchandising practices, and wants to know the returns, by reason of "Damaged", but based on location of display in the store, rather than category. This data is on the Inventory by Location report. I need to go pull the raw data of the Return Reason report (by item number), Pivot that with the Inventory by location report (by item number), and consolidate each reason code count by Location. The manager can now use hard data to put into his report on Changes to Merchandising to reduce Returns due to Damages. This report might be run over the next 6 months or so, to see if the proposed changes made a difference, and then will never be used again. It's this kind of stuff that the Excel whiz kid can do in about 1 hour, rather than having to go to IT, fill out a Request for System Modification form, go through 2-3 design meetings, create a BRD, get that approved by 2 or 3 business unit managers, go to an IT steering committee meeting to argue the priority of your report, and then, after 3 months of work, get told your report is too small of an impact to assign Development resources to it, and you turn to drinking heavily every happy hour to get through your work week.

So basically, learn Excel and avoid alcoholism. .~)

The internet itself can be controlled. The concept of a network cannot. If you want to run your own cables, and set up your own infrastructure, it can't be blocked, unless someone were to sabotage your stuff.

The internet consists of an (almost) unlimited number of uncontrollable ever-changing endpoints/servers. There is no good way you could ever hope to directly control that part.

However, the main "backbone" of our current internet is controlled by a very small number of companies. For example, say you live in Australia and want to connect to a site in Europe. While there are millions of possible start points in Australia and millions of possible endpoints in Europe, that connection still has to go through one of ~6 undersea cables to get there. So in that sense, it is already completely controlled.

Your question is slightly different and yes, you can have private servers that cannot (easily) be detected or blocked. However, the problem then becomes if it cannot be detected, how to do you tell people about it? And if it does become blocked, how do you tell people where it moved to? The answer to that question is your weak point where they'd attack/block/monitor/control.

No, it cannot.

There are two basic types of connections in networks. Client-server and peer-to-peer. Voat is an example of client server. You connect to a server and that server in turn delivers all your content to you. It's a single point of failure. If the company that hosts Voat decided they don't want to tomorrow then everything would be lost until the site could be moved to a new server and the process repeats.

Peer to peer is the other way. Torrents are (mostly) peer to peer. Instead of one server delivering all the content peers connect to each other and share content. Shutting down one peer doesn't do anything at all in terms of the availability of content.

In light of all the recent attacks on the internet ranging from censorship to increasingly invasive copyright measures many folks, including the scientists behind the original development of the internet, are starting to push for more decentralized and peer-to-peer type internet. The main reason this wasn't how things started is that client-server is just a whole lot easier. But outside of the initial technical implementations, peer to peer is vastly superior in just about every way. For instance it naturally scales. Think about client-server systems. When Voat saw massive growth the site began breaking simply because the server couldn't take it. But now think about a torrented file that's very popular. Lots of people torrent it but that means lots of people are also sharing it and so there's absolutely 0 impact on its availability. If anything as sites grow in a peer-to-peer environment they tend to become more reliable.

Peer to peer networks are impossible to shut down. Even if you killed off the internet as we know it (by, for instance disabling all ISPs), peer to peer networks would be able to rapidly and seamlessly migrate to begin developing a new internet using any sort of available and shared network capacity - such as wireless connections.
P2P could be easily blocked, if one were to attack the infrastructure connecting the the peers. The only truly resilient network is one you control

I'm not sure what you're trying to say or argue.

And like I mentioned even that would ultimately be insufficient as peer to peer technologies would work just as robustly in improvised systems which could ultimately culminate in an entirely peer to peer backbone as we have something like mesh nets connect to mesh nets.

Centralization or control is in general going to always be a bad idea since it's a single point of failure.

How do you think packets in peer to peer connections travel? I've got a hint, its the same way they travel in a client server structure. If the entity controlling the infrastructure it runs on wants to keep the traffic from going through, all it takes is a filter to block any traffic of whatever protocol you've designed.

Ah! Okay! That's not at all how the internet works.

The protocol and structure of internet connections are already specified. Software does not build its own outward protocol for network communications. An encrypted packet of information is just an encrypted packet of information. For an analogy imagine a postal company where all envelopes were the exact same size, form, etc. And if the postal company opened one of their letters there'd be nothing but gibberish in it - the only person who could decode the gibberish would be the recipient. So ISPs can see where something is coming from and where it's going although that can also be manipulated as, for instance, TOR does.

Blocking encrypted peer to peer traffic is impossible by this sort of means. Even for unencrypted traffic deep packet inspection is far from a silver bullet, and it would only effect the users whose ISP was engaging in such manipulation - not the entire decentralized network. But that's a bit of a side track - encryption alone nips this issue in the bud.

But your statement was that, should the entire internet get shut down, your peer to peer traffic could still get through. Your postman can still refuse to carry your damn letters. I was assuming unencrypted traffic here, for ease. I do fully admit that most of my work is not in networking. I'm a programmer who avoids writing netcode like the fucking plague, and all of my networking knowledge is considerably more of the broad "Design a functional network, and when your done with that, get outlook to sync with our new phones" type. So maybe my choice of words was not ideal. Point is, if you dont control every inch of the cable between you and who you want to be connected to, your traffic can be blocked. Doesn't mean there won't be a lot of innocent packets blocked too, of course.

Again, the postman can refuse to carry a single person's letters or just close their post office and stop delivering anybody's letters but these would have no real effect on the robustness of a peer to peer network. In a client-server system, if our postman decides to stop carrying any letters directed to or from voat then the site is for all intents and purposes dead. In a peer to peer system, nobody would even notice except for those who happened to be served by that post office at which point they could simply change servers.

I said the only way to completely disable a peer to peer network is to disable the entire internet. However, even that in the longrun would be insufficient. Check out mobile ad-hoc networks or mesh networks for a post-centralized internet. This isn't like esoteric 'gotchas', but major research is already ongoing to try to make progress on these fronts. At the recent decentralized web summit the keynote was given by no less than Tim Beners-Lee.
